s1-entitlement.title: S1 Entitlement
s1-entitlement.deliverables: Design, Service blueprint, problem framing workshops and interactive prototypes

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
The S1 entitlement allows UK pensioners and their dependants to access healthcare in EU countries, with the UK government covering treatment costs. However, the previous application process was manual and time-consuming—requiring users to apply by phone, submit documents by post, and wait for confirmation.

My role was to design a digital service that would streamline this process, making it easier for users to apply for and access their S1 certificate online, and reducing administrative burden on the NHS.

In addition, I designed a journey for internal Cost Recovery teams to log and reclaim NHS treatment costs for EU citizens receiving care in the UK.

sections.title: What was delivered
sections.html:
During discovery, I worked with a Business Analyst to map the current offline process and capture all caseworker interactions. This informed a detailed service design blueprint that structured the new digital journey, ensuring consistency with existing admin workflows.

I then designed and prototyped three linked services using the GOV.UK Design System:

  1. S1 application – a guided, eligibility-based journey to apply for S1 certification
  2. Evidence upload – allowing users to submit supporting documents
  3. Certificate download – enabling successful applicants to access their S1 digitally

I also developed an internal cost recovery flow, enabling NHS staff to record medical expenses for EU visitors—helping to reclaim funds from EU member states.

All services were tested with UK pensioners. Insights from usability testing led to several content and interaction improvements before final delivery.

sections.title: Deliverables included
sections.html:
• Service design blueprint mapping the full S1 entitlement process
  • Problem framing workshops to align stakeholders and define user needs
  • Interactive prototypes for S1 application, document upload, and certificate download
  • Internal cost recovery journey for NHS staff

generation-study.title: Generation study
generation-study.deliverables: User journey mapping, problem framing workshop and visual designs

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
The aim of Genomics England’s Generation Study is to identify rare genetic conditions in newborn babies by sequencing and analysing their genomes. The study could lead to earlier diagnoses, improved outcomes, and better quality of life for babies and their families.

My role was to design the Generation Study website—a platform where expectant parents could learn about the study and register their interest.

sections.title: What was delivered
sections.html:
Working alongside a content designer, I mapped out the user journey using insights from the discovery phase and a set of testable hypotheses. This led to the creation of low-fidelity wireframes that defined the site’s structure, navigation, key features, and interactions.

To support different user needs, we developed a content strategy using the paddle, swim, and dive model—offering varying levels of detail depending on how much users wanted to engage at each stage. This allowed the site to work for users wanting a quick overview, as well as those needing in-depth information before registering.

Using these wireframes, I designed the site in Figma, ensuring it was responsive across mobile, tablet, and desktop.

I also collaborated with the Genomics England brand team to create a tailored design system. This system balanced the organisation’s existing brand guidelines with new components and styling specific to the Generation Study, ensuring consistency during development.

We ran multiple usability testing sessions with prospective parents, iterating on the design based on feedback. The final prototypes were then handed over for development.

sections.title: Outputs included
sections.html:
• Responsive website designs across mobile, tablet, and desktop

  • A bespoke Generation Study design system (colours, typography, components, navigation)

  • Clickable Figma prototypes used for user testing and handoff

  • Journey maps and interaction flows based on real user needs and behaviours

btms.title: Border Trade Matching Service (BTMS)
btms.deliverables: Interaction and service design. Interactive prototypes

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
At DEFRA, I was the Lead Interaction Designer on the Border Trade Matching Service (BTMS) — a new internal service designed to replace a legacy system and support border and operational staff in making accurate, time-critical decisions on goods entering the UK from the EU and rest of world.

BTMS provides a search-led interface that allows users to find consignments using a range of reference numbers and view matched data from HMRC’s Customs Declaration Service (CDS) and IPAFFS in one place. This enables staff to quickly identify mismatches, understand why goods may be held, and enable staff to resolve issues to keep the border flowing.

The outcome was a service that made it easier for border teams to identify issues, understand what had happened, and take the right action.

sections.title: What was delivered
sections.html:
• Designed a search-led service allowing users to find consignments using multiple reference types
  • Created clear, scannable results views that bring together matched CDS and IPAFFS data in a single interface
  • Designed a consignment timeline to show key events, decisions, and status changes over time
  • Introduced visual indicators and filters to help users quickly identify discrepancies and prioritise action
  • Designed the BTMS reporting service, using visual graphs to show trends and operational data over time
  • Improved system messaging and error clarity to support faster issue resolution
  • Ensured accessibility and GOV.UK compliance, applying WCAG-aligned patterns and accessible data visualisation throughout

ipaffs.title: IPAFFS
ipaffs.deliverables: Interaction design, Service design and interactive prototypes

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
At DEFRA, I was the Lead Interaction Designer on IPAFFS (Import of Products, Animals, Food and Feed System) — the UK government service used to notify imports of regulated goods and live animals entering Great Britain.

My work focused on redesigning the CHED-A live animal import journey, reducing complexity in a high-risk, highly regulated process. Alongside a content designer we improved content clarity, simplified complex form interactions, and helped users understand what was required, when, and why. This included introducing clearer progress tracking, improving error handling, and supporting new online inspection fee payments — all designed and tested using GOV.UK design patterns.

The outcome was a simplified end-to-end journey that reduced user error in a high-risk import process by making complex regulatory requirements easier to understand and less onerous to complete.

sections.title: What was delivered
sections.html:
• Redesigned the CHED-A live animal import journey, reducing unnecessary steps and simplifying complex interactions such as commodity code selection

  • Introduced a notification hub, using the GOV.UK checklist pattern to help users track progress, save work, and return later with confidence

  • Designed a new payment journey to support online inspection fee payments within IPAFFS

  • Rebuilt the full IPAFFS prototype in Figma, using the GOV.UK prototyping toolkit to replace legacy Axure wireframes

  • Created a single, end-to-end testable prototype, enabling usability testing, service-wide gap analysis, and clearer stakeholder alignment
